title: Taxes & Assessments
overview: New York property taxes (assessment, equalization, levy and rate), exemptions including STAR, assessment challenges and unpaid taxes; the taxes due at a sale (transfer, mansion, NYC RPTT, mortgage recording, FIRPTA); and federal income tax rules: deductions, basis and gain, the §121 exclusion, depreciation and 1031 exchanges. Syllabus Subjects 14 and 17 (3 hours each, about 8% of the course) supply many math questions. Themes: apply the rate to taxable assessed value, divide by the equalization rate, know the grievance calendar and who pays which tax.

mustKnow: **Tax = taxable assessed value × rate**; **rate = levy ÷ total taxable assessed value**; **levy = budget − other revenue**. **New York State levies no property tax.**

Outside NYC and Nassau, all parcels share one **uniform percentage** of value (RPTL §305). **Full value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate**; the ORPTS rate apportions county and school levies and can exceed 100%.
Town calendar: **March 1** taxable status date → **May 1** tentative roll → **Grievance Day** (4th Tuesday in May) → **July 1** final roll → **30 days** to start SCAR or certiorari.

**Welcome stranger** assessing (raising only homes that just sold) is illegal and supports an **unequal** claim. A **special assessment** charges only benefited parcels, often by **front foot**; a **special district levy** is by value.

**Property tax liens** outrank private liens, even earlier mortgages. **In rem** foreclosure follows a redemption period of about **2 years**; since **Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023)** and NY's 2024 law, surplus goes to lienholders, then the former owner. A **tax lien sale** sells only the right to collect.

**STAR** cuts **school taxes** on a **primary residence** only. **Enhanced**: one resident owner **65 by December 31** and a lower income limit. New owners since **2016** get the **STAR credit**; switching from the exemption to the credit is **irreversible**.

Exemptions are **personal**. **Senior** (§467): up to **50%**, local option, combinable with Enhanced STAR. **Alternative veterans**: **15%** + **10%** combat + **half the disability rating**. Nonprofits need **exempt ownership and use**. Farmland converted within **5 years** (**8** outside an ag district) owes a **conversion payment**.

**Tax cap**: levy growth limited to **2% or inflation**; a school budget over it needs **60%**, and one bill can still rise more. **Homestead option**: two tax rates. **NYC class 1** (1–3 family): 6% ratio; caps of 6% a year, 20% over five.

Grievance grounds: **excessive, unequal, unlawful, misclassified**. **RP-524** must be **received** by Grievance Day; the BAR can't raise an assessment. **SCAR** (owner-occupied 1–3 family): **30 days**, **$30**; other property uses **Article 7 certiorari**. NYC: **Tax Commission**; Nassau: **Assessment Review Commission**.

**NYS transfer tax**: **$2 per $500 or fraction**, **seller** (buyer if the seller doesn't pay). **Mansion tax**: **1% of the whole price** at **$1,000,000+**, **buyer**. **NYC RPTT**: **1%** up to $500,000, **1.425% of the whole price** above.
**Mortgage recording tax** is on the **loan**: none for cash buyers or co-op share loans; a **CEMA** taxes only **new money**.

**FIRPTA**: the buyer withholds **15% of the gross price** from a foreign seller (**10%** for a buyer-occupied home at $300,001–$1,000,000; none at $300,000 or less). Nonresident sellers pay NY estimated tax on **IT-2663**.

Mortgage interest (debt up to **$750,000**, now permanent) and property taxes (SALT cap **$40,000** for 2025, **$40,400** for 2026) help only **itemizers**; home-equity interest counts only if the loan buys, builds or improves the home; **mortgage insurance** is deductible again from 2026.

**§121**: exclude **$250,000/$500,000** after owning and using the home **2 of the last 5 years**; once every 2 years, any age. **Gain** = amount realized − adjusted basis; a mortgage payoff is irrelevant.
**Depreciation**: buildings only, never land or a personal home; **27.5 years** residential rental, **39** nonresidential; gain from past depreciation is taxed at up to **25%**.
**1031**: investment real estate for investment real estate; **45 / 180 days**, both from the sale; a **qualified intermediary** holds the cash; boot is taxed; gain is deferred.
**Inherited** property gets a **stepped-up** basis; a **gift** keeps the donor's basis. **Long-term** means held **more than 1 year**.

traps.trap: To get full value, multiply the assessment by the equalization rate.
An equalization rate can never top 100%.
traps.truth: It can, when values fall and assessments aren't lowered. Some study guides wrongly say otherwise.
March 1 is the taxable status date; Grievance Day in most towns is the fourth Tuesday in May.

traps.trap: A grievance mailed by Grievance Day is on time, and owners can skip it and sue or stop paying.
traps.truth: The RP-524 must be received by Grievance Day and is required before SCAR or certiorari. Withholding taxes only adds a lien and penalties.

traps.trap: A mortgage recorded first beats a later tax lien.
traps.truth: Property tax liens outrank private liens regardless of date, which is why lenders escrow taxes.

traps.trap: The buyer keeps the seller's STAR, senior or veterans exemption.
traps.truth: Exemptions are personal; the buyer must qualify and apply on her own.

traps.trap: Enhanced STAR requires both spouses, or all owners, to be 65.
traps.truth: Since 2026, one resident owner 65 by December 31 is enough, whatever the owners' relationship. The older all-owners rule is outdated.

traps.trap: The 2% tax cap means no bill can rise more than 2%.
traps.truth: It limits the total levy (with a 60% override). One bill can rise more after a reassessment or a lost exemption.

traps.trap: NYC RPTT on a $750,000 condo is 1% on the first $500,000 and 1.425% on the rest.
traps.truth: It isn't tiered: 1.425% × $750,000 = $10,687.50. The mansion tax likewise hits the whole price.

traps.trap: The state transfer tax starts above $25,000 and is exactly 0.4%.
traps.truth: It applies above $500 at $2 per $500 or fraction, rounding up. $25,000 is the NYC RPTT floor.

traps.trap: Mortgage recording tax is a percentage of the price, and co-op buyers pay it too.
traps.truth: It is figured on the recorded loan; cash buyers and co-op share loans pay none.

traps.trap: The home-sale exclusion is a one-time break for sellers 55+ who buy a pricier home.
traps.truth: That ended in 1997. Anyone meeting the 2-of-5-year tests can exclude $250,000 or $500,000 once every 2 years, without reinvesting.

traps.trap: Paying off the mortgage at closing reduces the taxable gain.
traps.truth: It only reduces the seller's cash. Gain = amount realized − adjusted basis.

traps.trap: FIRPTA withholding is 15% of the seller's profit.
traps.truth: It is 15% of the gross amount realized, and a buyer who fails to withhold can be liable.

traps.trap: A 1031 exchange is tax-free, and the 180 days start after the 45 days end.
traps.truth: It defers gain (the replacement takes a lower basis), and both clocks start at the sale. Homes and dealer property don't qualify.

traps.trap: The SALT cap is still $10,000, and mortgage insurance is never deductible.
traps.truth: The 2025 law set $40,000 for 2025 and $40,400 for 2026 (phased down at high incomes, never below $10,000), and mortgage insurance is deductible again from 2026.

mnemonics.name: PETE
mnemonics.meaning: Government's four powers over private property: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat

formulas.name: Property tax
formulas.formula: Tax = taxable assessed value × rate (mills ÷ 1,000; per $100 ÷ 100)

formulas.name: Assessed value and full value
formulas.formula: AV = market value × level of assessment; full value = AV ÷ equalization rate

formulas.name: Mortgage recording tax
formulas.formula: Loan amount × combined rate (CEMA: new money only)

formulas.formula: (Price − selling costs) − (cost + capitalized costs + improvements − depreciation)

formulas.name: 1031 boot and basis
formulas.formula: Taxed now = lesser of boot or realized gain; new basis = replacement cost − deferred gain
formulas.example: Gain $220,000, boot $40,000 → $40,000 taxed; $1,000,000 replacement − $180,000 deferred = $820,000 basis

formulas.name: Installment sale
formulas.formula: Gain reported = principal received × (gross profit ÷ contract price)

formulas.name: FIRPTA
formulas.formula: 15% × amount realized (10% for a $300,001–$1,000,000 home the buyer will occupy; none at $300,000 or less)

formulas.name: After-tax cash flow
formulas.formula: Tax = (NOI − interest − depreciation) × rate; ATCF = NOI − debt service − tax

sections.heading: How property taxes work
sections.intro: Property taxes are the main source of local revenue. First identify who levies a charge and what kind it is.
points: Property taxes fund local services: schools (usually the largest share), police, fire, roads, libraries and parks. **Taxation** is the T in PETE.
Counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts and special districts levy them. **New York State levies none.**
Real estate is taxed because it is a **predictable** base, **hard to conceal** or move, and historically tied to **wealth and land productivity**.
**Ad valorem** means 'according to value': taxable assessed value × rate on every taxable parcel. A transfer tax is due only on a conveyance.

An **assessing unit** (usually a city or town; Nassau and Tompkins counties assess countywide) keeps the **assessment roll**; school and other districts, whose lines can cross town lines, levy from it.
Wholly **exempt property** (government, religious, charitable, educational) pays no general tax, shifting the burden to other owners.

A **special assessment** charges only benefited parcels (a **special assessment district**) for one improvement, such as sidewalks or a sewer line, usually by front footage. It is a **specific lien**, often paid in installments, and adds to basis rather than being deducted. A **special district** (fire, water, sewer, lighting) levies by value inside its boundaries.

example.title: Worked example: special assessment by front foot
steps: New curbs cost $96,000 along a street with 1,600 total front feet. A lot is 60 feet wide (frontage) and 120 feet deep.
Step 1: Cost per front foot = $96,000 ÷ 1,600 = $60.
Step 2: Charge = 60 × $60 = $3,600, a specific lien until paid. Using the 120-foot depth ($7,200) is the trap.

sections.heading: Assessment, the assessment calendar, and reassessment
sections.intro: The assessor values property and fixes factual errors; the receiver of taxes collects; the governing body (and school voters) adopts the budget.
points: **Market (full) value** is the likely sale price; **assessed value** is the roll figure; **taxable assessed value** is assessed value minus exemptions and can differ for county, town and school taxes.

**Uniform percentage** (RPTL §305): outside NYC and Nassau, every parcel is assessed at one percentage of value, 100% or any fraction; only those two use class percentages. **Level of assessment** = assessed value ÷ market value; with no required reassessment cycle, many towns sit far below 100%.

Town calendar: **valuation date** July 1 of the prior year (fixes market conditions) → **taxable status date** March 1 (fixes condition, ownership and exemption eligibility; applications due) → **tentative roll** May 1 → **Grievance Day**, the fourth Tuesday in May → **final roll** July 1 → **30 days** to start SCAR or certiorari.

Assessments drift: values change unevenly, **new construction** enters at current value while older homes keep stale values, and **undeclared improvements** stay off the roll until **building permits** alert the assessor.
A **community-wide reassessment** redistributes the levy but doesn't raise it: when total assessed value rises and the levy doesn't, the rate falls.

Raising only homes that just sold (**welcome stranger** assessing) is illegal and supports an **unequal** grievance; a town-wide revaluation, adding a newly found improvement or correcting an error is legal.

**Back taxes** are limited: RPTL §551 adds property omitted from the prior year's roll, at that year's rate; there's no general ten-year rule. Exempt property bought by a non-exempt owner is taxed at once, prorated (RPTL §520; STAR excepted).

example.title: Worked example: a revaluation with the levy unchanged
steps: A $3,000,000 levy on $60,000,000 of taxable value is $50 per $1,000; owners A and B, each assessed at $24,000, pay $1,200.
Step 1: A revaluation raises the total to $240,000,000, so the rate falls to $12.50 per $1,000.
Step 2: A rises 4 times, like the town, to $96,000: still $1,200. Under-assessed B rises 5 times, to $120,000: $1,500.
Answer: the levy didn't grow; the burden shifted to B. Keeping the old $50 rate is the trap.

sections.heading: Equalization rates and the residential assessment ratio
sections.intro: Equalization puts towns that assess at different percentages on a common full-value basis.
points: The **state equalization rate** = a municipality's total assessed value ÷ total market value. **ORPTS** (Department of Taxation and Finance) sets it from sales data, such as the **RP-5217** filed with each deed.
Its main job is **apportioning county and school levies**: convert each town's assessed value to full value, then split the levy by share of full value.

**Full value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate**; never multiply. The rate can **exceed 100%** when values fall; a falling rate with unchanged assessments means values rose. It describes a whole municipality, not anyone's bill.

The **residential assessment ratio (RAR)** compares residential assessments with residential market values. At the BAR or in SCAR, a home whose assessment ÷ market value exceeds the RAR is unequally assessed.

example.title: Worked example: apportioning a county levy
steps: A county must raise $9,000,000. Town A: $60,000,000 assessed, rate 40%. Town B: $210,000,000, rate 70%.
Trap: splitting by raw assessed value (60 ÷ 270) charges A only $2,000,000, rewarding the town that assesses lower.

sections.heading: From budget to tax bill
sections.intro: Assessments set each owner's share; the budget sets how much there is to share.
points: An **appropriation** authorizes spending; the budget totals them. **Levy** = budget − other revenue (state aid, sales tax share, fees).

**Rate** = levy ÷ total **taxable** assessed value; leaving exempt property out raises everyone else's rate. Rates appear as decimals, percents, dollars per $100 or $1,000, or **mills**; to compare, convert to per $1,000 (per $100 × 10; percent × 10).
**Tax = taxable assessed value × rate**, never market value × rate. Each bill line (county, town, school, village, district) has its own rate and exemptions.
**Agent responsibility**: compute taxes from the current roll and rates, note which exemptions the bill reflects, and never present the seller's bill as the buyer's future tax.

example.title: Worked example: from budget to one owner's tax
steps: Budget $14,200,000; state aid and fees $5,200,000; roll $320,000,000, including $20,000,000 wholly exempt.

sections.heading: Exemptions: STAR, seniors, veterans, farmland, and nonprofits
sections.intro: Exemptions lower taxable assessed value (the STAR credit is a check instead). Most need an application by the taxable status date and belong to the owner: a buyer must qualify and apply anew.
points: **Wholly exempt**: government property and nonprofit religious, charitable, educational and hospital property (RPTL §420-a) with **exempt ownership and exempt use**; a floor a church leases to a for-profit firm is taxable.

**STAR** cuts **school taxes only**, on a **primary residence** only. **Basic**: no age test; income up to $500,000 (credit) or $250,000 (exemption). **Enhanced**: one resident owner (since 2026, whatever the owners' relationship) **65 by December 31** of the benefit year, and resident owners' and spouses' income of $110,750 or less (2026; $113,550 for 2027). Upgrades to Enhanced are automatic.

**Credit vs exemption**: new homeowners since 2016 register with the Tax Department for the **STAR credit** (check or direct deposit); the school-bill exemption is closed to newcomers. Switching from exemption to credit is **irreversible**; only the credit can grow (up to 2% a year).

**Senior citizens exemption** (RPTL §467; local option for each county, city, town, village and school district): up to **50%** off for owners 65+ under the local income limit (an added option reaches 65% at the lowest incomes). All owners must be 65 unless they are spouses or siblings (then one), and they must have owned the home 12 months. It combines with Enhanced STAR.

**Alternative veterans exemption** (§458-a; local option, schools included): 15% wartime + 10% combat zone + half the service-connected disability rating, under local caps; no special district relief. **Cold War** and **eligible funds** exemptions are separate. Where adopted, VA-rated **permanently and totally disabled** veterans get a **full** exemption on their primary residence, special levies and assessments included, on rolls with taxable status dates from **October 1, 2026** (§458-a(11)).
**Disabilities and limited incomes** (§459-c): up to 50% by local option; owners eligible for this and the senior exemption choose one.

**Agricultural assessment** (Agriculture and Markets Law §305) taxes farmland at farm value. Converting it within **5 years** (**8** outside an agricultural district) triggers a **conversion payment** (five times the last year's savings plus interest); idling land doesn't.

example.title: Worked example: a veterans exemption, then a sale
steps: A combat-zone wartime veteran rated 40% disabled owns a home assessed at $200,000; the town rate is 24 mills and caps aren't reached.
Step 3: A non-veteran buyer pays on $200,000: $4,800, because the exemption is personal.

sections.heading: Tax cap, homestead option, and NYC and Nassau classes
sections.intro: The levy cap, the two-rate homestead option, and the NYC and Nassau class systems change how the tax burden is divided.
points: The **property tax cap** (General Municipal Law §3-c; Education Law §2023-a; permanent since 2019) limits levy growth to **2% or inflation**, whichever is less, with adjustments. A school budget above it needs **60%** voter approval; a local government overrides by a local law passed by 60% of its board. NYC isn't covered.

**Homestead option** (RPTL Article 19): an **approved assessing unit** that completed a state-recognized revaluation may tax **homestead** (mostly 1–3 family) and **non-homestead** property at different rates, so homeowners don't absorb more after a revaluation. Assessments stay uniform.

NYC and Nassau are **special assessing units** with classes (RPTL Article 18), each with its own ratio and rate. NYC assesses class 1 at **6%** of market value and the rest at 45%; its tax year runs July 1–June 30.

NYC caps market-driven class 1 increases at **6% a year and 20% over five years**, and class 2 buildings of 10 or fewer units at 8% and 30%; larger class 2 and class 4 phase changes in over five years. Physical improvements aren't capped.
Co-op owners pay through maintenance (the building is one class 2 parcel); condo units are assessed individually.

example.title: Worked example: the NYC class 1 cap
steps: A Staten Island two-family house was assessed at $28,000 last year; 6% of Finance's new market value is $36,000, with no physical change.
Trap: the small class 2 cap (8%) gives $30,240; the 20% five-year cap in one year gives $33,600. A new addition would be added outside the cap.

sections.heading: Challenging an assessment: grievance, SCAR, and certiorari
sections.intro: Owners challenge the assessment, not the budget: informal review, then grievance, then court.
points: **Grounds** (RPTL §§522, 524): **excessive** (above full value, or a partial exemption denied), **unequal** (a higher level of assessment than comparable property), **unlawful** (e.g., exempt property assessed as taxable) and **misclassified**. A disliked budget isn't one.

**Grievance**: **Form RP-524** must be **received** by the assessor before, or the **Board of Assessment Review (BAR)** on, **Grievance Day** (4th Tuesday in May in most towns; Suffolk towns 3rd Tuesday in May, Westchester towns 3rd Tuesday in June); mailing in time isn't enough. The BAR has 3–5 appointed members, never the assessor or staff.

Evidence: comparable sales, an appraisal, similar homes' assessments, the level of assessment or RAR, condition. The BAR may **deny**, **grant** or **grant in part**, never raise. Taxes stay due; a win brings a refund.

**SCAR**: owner-occupied 1–3 family homes used only as residences (and lots too small to build on) claiming unequal or excessive assessment. File with the county clerk within **30 days** after the final roll (or notice of its filing, if later); **$30**; no lawyer needed. A hearing officer weighs sales, assessment and ratio evidence; outcomes match the BAR's.

SCAR limits: equalized value of $450,000 or less (otherwise a cut of no more than 25%), and no lower assessment than was requested at the BAR. Filing SCAR waives certiorari; review is only by **Article 78**.

example.title: Worked example: what assessment to request
steps: A town assesses at 50%. A home is assessed at $210,000; sales support $360,000; the rate is $32 per $1,000.
Step 1: Implied value = $210,000 ÷ 0.50 = $420,000, $60,000 too high.
Trap: subtracting the whole $60,000 gap ($150,000) ignores the 50% level.

sections.heading: Tax liens, tax sales, and in rem foreclosure
sections.intro: Unpaid property taxes survive a sale; they attach to the parcel.
points: Unpaid taxes become a **specific, involuntary lien** that outranks private liens, even earlier mortgages; lenders escrow taxes and title searches check for them.
**In rem** ('against the thing'): an **RPTL Article 11** foreclosure targets the parcel, not the owner personally, and reaches homes as well as commercial property.

**Redemption**: the owner can pay taxes, interest and charges until the period ends, generally **two years after the lien date** (longer by local law for residential or farm property; one year for listed vacant and abandoned homes). Then the court can award title to the tax district.

**Surplus**: **Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023)** held that keeping more than the tax debt is a taking. New York's 2024 law (RPTL §§1196–1197) makes the district pay any surplus into court (the public-sale price, or full value if not sold publicly, minus taxes, interest and charges); lienholders, then the former owner, claim it.

**Tax lien sale** (NYC and some other places): an investor buys the right to collect the taxes plus interest. It isn't a transfer of title: the owner keeps title and can pay off the lien until a later foreclosure.
**Agent duty**: confirm taxes are current and flag liens or pending tax sales early; delinquent taxes are paid from the seller's proceeds.

sections.heading: Transfer taxes and mortgage recording tax
sections.intro: Transfer taxes are figured on the price; the mortgage recording tax on the loan.
points: **NYS transfer tax** (Tax Law §1402): **$2 per $500 or fraction** (about 0.4%) above $500 of consideration; round partial units up. The **seller** pays; if the seller doesn't or is exempt, the **buyer** must. It's reported on **Form TP-584**, due within 15 days of the deed's delivery.

**Mansion tax** (§1402-a): **1% of the entire price** when a residence (1–3 family house, condo or co-op unit) sells for **$1,000,000 or more**, paid by the **buyer**; exactly $1,000,000 owes $10,000.

**NYC extras** (since July 1, 2019): the state base rate is 0.65% for NYC residences of $3 million+ and other NYC property of $2 million+ (seller); NYC residences of $2 million+ owe a **supplemental mansion tax** of 0.25% to 2.9% (buyer).

**NYC RPTT**: on NYC transfers over $25,000. Residential: **1%** at $500,000 or less, **1.425% of the whole price** above; other property 1.425% or 2.625%. The seller normally pays, on top of the state tax.

No state transfer tax on gifts, inheritances, deeds that only secure a debt, or correction deeds. Co-op sales are taxed; a co-op **flip tax** is a private building fee. Some localities (Yonkers, the Peconic Bay towns) add their own transfer taxes.

**Mortgage recording tax** (Tax Law Article 11) is on the recorded **loan**, per $100 (a remainder over $50 counts as $100); cash buyers pay none. It combines a basic 0.50%, a special additional 0.25% (paid by the **lender** on 1–6 family homes), an additional 0.25% (0.30% in the NYC-area commuter counties), with the first $10,000 of a 1–2 family loan excluded from it, and local taxes in NYC, Yonkers and some counties.

Suburban commuter counties typically total 1.05%; NYC borrowers pay 1.8% on 1–3 family or condo loans under $500,000 and 1.925% at $500,000 or more. Exam problems usually just multiply the loan by a given rate.
**Co-op share loans** pay none (no real property mortgage is recorded). A **CEMA** assigns the old mortgage to the new lender so only the **new money** is taxed (Tax Law §255).

example.title: Worked example: closing taxes on a Brooklyn condo
steps: A Brooklyn condo sells for $1,200,000; the buyer records a $900,000 mortgage at a stated borrower rate of 1.925%.
Step 1: NYS transfer tax = 2,400 units × $2 = $4,800 (seller).
Step 2: NYC RPTT = 1.425% × $1,200,000 = $17,100 (seller); mansion tax = $12,000 (buyer). The NYC supplemental tax starts at $2,000,000.
Step 3: Mortgage tax = $900,000 × 1.925% = $17,325 (buyer); taxing the price is the trap.
Step 4: A later CEMA refinance from a $700,000 balance to $800,000 taxes only the $100,000 of new money.
Answer: seller $21,900; buyer $29,325.

sections.heading: Homeowner income tax: deductions and limits
sections.intro: A home affects income tax mainly through itemized deductions; state the rules accurately and refer specifics to a tax professional.
points: Mortgage interest and property taxes are **itemized deductions**, useful only when itemizing beats the **standard deduction**.

**Acquisition debt** (to buy, build or substantially improve the main home or one second home): interest on up to **$750,000** is deductible for loans after December 15, 2017 ($1,000,000 for older loans). The 2025 federal tax law (P.L. 119-21) made $750,000 permanent.

**Home equity** interest qualifies only if the money buys, builds or substantially improves the home securing it, not credit cards, tuition or a car. A refinance stays acquisition debt up to the old balance plus improvement money; a home under construction qualifies for up to 24 months.

**Points** to buy a main home are generally deductible when paid (seller-paid points too, but they lower the buyer's basis); refinance points are spread over the loan. A **prepayment penalty** counts as interest. **Mortgage insurance premiums** are deductible again from 2026, phased out between $100,000 and $109,000 of AGI.

The **SALT cap** covers property taxes plus state and local income (or sales) taxes: $10,000 for 2018–2024, then **$40,000** for 2025 and **$40,400** for 2026 (1% more yearly through 2029), cut by 30% of MAGI over $500,000 ($505,000 in 2026) but never below $10,000; back to $10,000 in 2030. Married filing separately: half.
Sale year: the seller deducts taxes through the day before closing, the buyer from closing on, whoever paid the town; a buyer's proration credit counts as the buyer paying.

**Not deductible**: principal, homeowners insurance, HOA or condo charges, utilities, repairs, personal-home depreciation, transfer taxes and special assessments (the last two adjust basis or the amount realized).
Co-op owners deduct their share of building interest and taxes paid through maintenance (IRC §216). New York allows itemizing on the state return without itemizing federally.
**IRA first home**: up to **$10,000** lifetime avoids the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, but a traditional IRA withdrawal is still taxed; first-time means no main home owned in the prior 2 years.
**Vacation home**: interest on one second home counts within the $750,000 limit; rent for fewer than 15 days a year isn't reported.

example.title: Worked example: who deducts the property taxes in the sale year
steps: The seller paid the $7,300 calendar-year town tax in January. Closing is April 1 (not a leap year); the buyer owns the closing day.
Step 2: Seller: January 1–March 31 = 90 days = $1,800. Buyer: April 1–December 31 = 275 days = $5,500, credited to the seller.
Answer: each deducts its own share (if itemizing), though the seller paid the town.

sections.heading: Basis, gain, and the home-sale exclusion (§121)
sections.intro: Gain is measured against adjusted basis, not the price or the mortgage. The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 created today's exclusion.
points: **Basis** = price + capitalized purchase costs (owner's title insurance, recording and legal fees, survey, buyer-paid transfer tax, seller's back taxes the buyer paid). Loan costs and insurance premiums aren't added.

**Adjusted basis** = basis + **capital improvements** − depreciation. An improvement adds value, extends life or adapts the property (addition, new roof, central air, garage, sidewalk assessment); a **repair** (painting, fixing a leak) doesn't count.

**Amount realized** = price − selling costs (commission, legal fees, seller-paid transfer tax, which isn't deductible); **gain** = amount realized − adjusted basis. A mortgage payoff changes cash, not gain.

**§121**: exclude up to **$250,000** ($500,000 joint) if the seller **owned** and **used** the home as a main home **2 of the 5 years** before the sale; the months needn't be consecutive or the same for both tests. Usable **once every 2 years**, at any age, with no reinvestment; the age-55 one-time exclusion and rollover ended in 1997.

**Joint**: either spouse may meet ownership, but **both** must meet use and neither may have used the exclusion in the prior 2 years; otherwise each qualifying spouse gets up to $250,000. An unmarried surviving spouse keeps $500,000 for a sale within 2 years of the death.
**Reduced exclusion** (job change, health, unforeseen circumstances): maximum × qualifying months ÷ 24.

Not excluded: gain equal to depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 (home office, rental), gain allocated to post-2008 rental use before the home became the main home, and gain on a home acquired by 1031 exchange and sold within 5 years. A **loss** on a personal home isn't deductible; an investment capital loss offsets gains plus $3,000 a year of other income.

**Inherited** property gets a **stepped-up basis** (value at death) and is automatically long-term; a **gift** keeps the donor's **carryover basis**. **Long-term** gain (held more than 1 year) is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%; short-term at ordinary rates.

example.title: Worked example: gain and the exclusion
steps: A single owner paid $310,000 plus $4,000 of title, recording and legal costs, added a $40,000 kitchen and $16,000 roof, and spent $5,000 repainting. Seven years later she sold for $720,000 with $42,000 of selling costs, paying off a $200,000 mortgage.
Step 1: Adjusted basis = $310,000 + $4,000 + $40,000 + $16,000 = $370,000 (painting excluded).
Step 2: Gain = ($720,000 − $42,000) − $370,000 = $308,000; the mortgage plays no part.
Step 3: She meets the 2-of-5 tests: $308,000 − $250,000 = $58,000 taxable long-term gain. A qualifying married couple filing jointly would owe nothing.

sections.heading: Investment property: depreciation, taxable income, and sale
sections.intro: Rentals are taxed like a business: rent is income; expenses and depreciation are deductions; and depreciation lowers basis, raising the gain at sale.
points: Income types: **active** (wages, commissions, a business the owner materially runs), **passive** (rentals, businesses without material participation), **portfolio** (interest, dividends, securities gains). Passive losses generally offset only passive income and carry forward until sale.

Exceptions: an actively participating landlord may deduct up to **$25,000** of rental losses, phased out between $100,000 and $150,000 of income; an IRS **real estate professional** (750+ hours and over half of working time in real estate, materially participating) isn't limited. A license alone doesn't qualify.

**Depreciation**: a yearly deduction for buildings and improvements used in business or held for income; **land** and a **personal residence** never qualify. Straight-line: **27.5 years** residential rental (80%+ of rents from dwelling units, so an 85% apartment building qualifies in full), **39 years** nonresidential, on cost − land; exam problems ignore the partial first year.

Depreciation is a non-cash **tax shelter**, lowering taxable income and basis even as the building appreciates. **Taxable income** = NOI − interest − depreciation (principal isn't deductible); **after-tax cash flow** = NOI − debt service − tax.
At a sale, gain equal to past depreciation (**unrecaptured §1250 gain**, the recapture portion) is taxed at up to **25%**; the rest is long-term capital gain.
**Installment sale** (seller financing): gain is reported as principal arrives, at principal × (gross profit ÷ contract price); interest is ordinary income.
**LIHTC**: federal low-income housing credits, allocated by housing agencies, cut tax dollar for dollar over 10 years, with a 15-year compliance period.

example.title: Worked example: depreciation, cash flow, and gain
steps: A rental duplex costs $520,000, including $107,500 of land. NOI is $40,000; interest $20,000; principal $6,000; 24% bracket.
Step 1: Depreciation = ($520,000 − $107,500) ÷ 27.5 = $15,000 (not $18,909 on the full cost).
Step 3: After 8 years, basis = $520,000 − $120,000 = $400,000; a $640,000 net sale gains $240,000: $120,000 (the depreciation) taxed at up to 25%, $120,000 as long-term capital gain.

sections.heading: Section 1031 like-kind exchanges
sections.intro: A 1031 exchange rolls gain from one investment property into another; the tax is deferred, not forgiven.
points: **Eligible**: real property held for business or investment, exchanged for like-kind real property held the same way; since 2018, only real property.

**Like-kind** is broad: rental houses, apartments, offices, industrial buildings, hotels and investment land are interchangeable, and a leasehold with 30+ years left is like-kind to ownership. U.S. and foreign property aren't.
**Not eligible**: a personal or personally used vacation home, dealer property (a builder's lots, a flipper's houses), stocks and partnership interests.

**Deadlines**: identify in writing within **45 days**; acquire within **180 days** or by the return due date (with extensions), if earlier. Both run from the sale, concurrently, with no weekend extension. Identify up to three properties (more under the 200% rule).

A **qualified intermediary** holds the proceeds; if the investor receives the cash, the exchange fails. The investor's agent, attorney or broker within the past 2 years can't serve; there's no advance IRS approval.

**Boot** = cash, other property or **net debt relief**; recognized gain = the lesser of boot or realized gain. Full deferral needs equal or greater value, all equity reinvested, and debt replaced or offset with cash.
**New basis** = replacement cost − deferred gain. In a **reverse exchange** the replacement is bought first and parked with an accommodation titleholder, under the same deadlines.

head: Topic
Rule
Trap
rows: A home or flip doesn't qualify
Both run from the sale, not one after the other
Taking the proceeds ends the exchange
Cash, other property, net debt relief
Debt relief counts even with no cash
Using full cost erases the deferred gain

example.title: Worked example: deadlines, boot, and basis
steps: A building with a $300,000 adjusted basis closes October 2, 2026 for $800,000 net; the investor buys a $750,000 replacement and keeps $50,000.
Step 1: Identify by November 16, 2026; acquire by March 31, 2027, before the April 15 return due date.
Step 2: Gain = $500,000; the $50,000 boot is taxed now and $450,000 deferred.

sections.heading: FIRPTA and nonresident sellers
sections.intro: Two rules can cut a seller's cash at a New York closing: FIRPTA for foreign sellers and NY estimated tax for nonresidents. A foreign seller can face both.
points: **FIRPTA** (IRC §1445): when a **foreign person** sells U.S. real property, the **buyer** withholds **15% of the amount realized** (gross price, not gain) and remits it on Forms 8288 and 8288-A within **20 days**; a buyer who fails to withhold can be liable.

**Residence exceptions**, if an individual buyer plans to live there at least half the days it's used in each of the first two years: **none** at $300,000 or less; **10%** at $300,001–$1,000,000. Any other foreign-seller sale: 15%.
A U.S. seller's **certification of non-foreign status** ends the duty. A foreign seller can seek an IRS withholding certificate for less; withholding is credited against the actual tax.

**NY nonresident sellers** (individuals, estates and trusts, foreign sellers included) pay estimated NY tax on the gain at closing on **Form IT-2663** (IT-2664 for co-ops), filed with the TP-584; the clerk won't record the deed without it. It's the seller's payment, not withholding, and a fully qualifying §121 sale is exempt.
**Agent duty**: ask early whether the seller is foreign or a nonresident.

example.title: Worked example: FIRPTA on a condo sale
steps: A foreign individual sells a condo for $650,000.
Step 1: To an investor: 15% × $650,000 = $97,500.
Step 2: To a buyer who will live there: 10% = $65,000; at $290,000, nothing. Taking 15% of the gain is the trap.
